medium.conteudo_html:
Artificial intelligence has changed the way people work, communicate, research, create content, analyze information, and solve everyday business problems. Tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini can help professionals write emails, summarize documents, develop marketing ideas, analyze data, create business plans, generate content, and handle repetitive tasks in a fraction of the time traditional methods require.

Yet there is a major difference between simply using an AI tool and using it effectively.

Many professionals open an AI chatbot, type a short request, receive an average answer, and assume that the technology is limited. In reality, the quality of the result often depends heavily on the quality of the instructions given to the AI.

This is where prompt engineering becomes valuable.

You do not need to be a software developer, programmer, data scientist, or AI researcher to use prompt engineering. For marketers, consultants, entrepreneurs, freelancers, managers, writers, educators, and other knowledge workers, prompt engineering is increasingly becoming a practical workplace skill.

A well-designed prompt can turn a vague AI response into a structured research brief, a useful marketing strategy, a polished customer email, a detailed content plan, or a practical business analysis.

That is the purpose behind Prompt Engineering for the AI Era + Toolkit E-books: providing a practical digital resource for non-technical professionals who want to get better and faster results from modern AI tools without needing a technical background.

What Is Prompt Engineering?

Prompt engineering is the practice of creating clear, structured instructions that guide an AI model toward a useful result.

A prompt can be very simple:

“Write a blog post about email marketing.”

However, this request leaves many important questions unanswered.

Who is the audience? What is the purpose of the article? What tone should be used? How long should it be? What information should it include? Should it be optimized for search engines? What action should readers take afterward?

A more structured prompt could specify the audience, objective, tone, format, length, key points, and limitations.

The difference is significant.

Prompt engineering is not about finding magical words that make AI perfect. It is about communicating your goal clearly enough that an AI system has useful context for producing the type of response you actually need.

This makes prompt engineering particularly relevant for professionals who already have industry knowledge but do not have technical AI skills.

Why Prompt Engineering Matters for Non-Technical Professionals

The modern workplace produces enormous amounts of information.

Professionals read emails, reports, proposals, research papers, customer feedback, meeting notes, sales data, product documentation, social media comments, and internal communications.

AI can help process much of this information, but the professional still needs to explain what the AI should do with it.

Consider a consultant who wants to analyze customer feedback.

A basic prompt might be:

“Analyze these customer comments.”

A stronger prompt could say:

“Analyze the customer comments below. Group them into five major themes, identify recurring complaints, separate positive feedback from negative feedback, estimate which issues appear most frequently, and finish with five practical recommendations for improving the customer experience. Present the results in a table.”

The second prompt provides a clear task, output structure, and decision-making context.

That means less time correcting the AI response and more time using the result.

For busy professionals, that distinction can translate into meaningful productivity gains.

ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini: Why Better Prompts Matter

Modern AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are capable of handling a wide range of professional tasks.

They can assist with:

· Writing and editing

· Brainstorming

· Research organization

· Business analysis

· Marketing

· Customer communication

· Content creation

· Summarization

· Translation

· Data interpretation

· Strategic planning

· Project documentation

· Learning and training

· Coding assistance

· Workflow development

The specific features and capabilities of each AI platform can change over time, but one principle remains useful across systems: clear instructions generally produce more useful outputs than vague instructions.

This makes transferable prompting skills more valuable than memorizing hundreds of isolated prompts.

A professional who understands how to define a role, provide context, specify constraints, request a format, and review the result can adapt those techniques across different AI platforms.

The Basic Anatomy of a Strong AI Prompt

A useful prompt does not always need to be long.

In many situations, five elements are enough:

1. Role

Tell the AI what perspective or professional function it should use.

For example:

“Act as a B2B content strategist…”

or:

“Act as a customer support manager…”

A role can establish the type of reasoning and language that fits the task.

2. Context

Explain the situation.

Instead of:

“Write a sales email.”

Try:

“We sell project management software to small professional services firms. The recipient downloaded our productivity guide but has not requested a demo.”

The AI now has useful background information.

3. Task

Clearly state what needs to be done.

For example:

“Write a short follow-up email that explains the product’s main benefit and encourages the recipient to schedule a demonstration.”

4. Constraints

Define boundaries.

You might specify:

· Word count

· Tone

· Reading level

· Audience

· Number of options

· Topics to avoid

· Required information

· Brand guidelines

5. Output Format

Tell the AI how the response should be organized.

For example:

“Return the answer as a three-column table with Problem, Recommendation, and Expected Business Impact.”

These five elements create a practical framework that can be reused across hundreds of professional tasks.

Prompt Engineering for Marketing Professionals

Marketing teams are among the biggest beneficiaries of effective AI prompting.

AI can support many stages of the marketing process, but the output becomes more useful when the prompt contains specific business information.

A marketer can use AI prompts for:

· Customer personas

· SEO keyword research

· Blog outlines

· Social media content

· Email campaigns

· Product descriptions

· Ad copy

· Landing pages

· Content calendars

· Competitor analysis

· Customer surveys

· Campaign ideas

· A/B testing concepts

For example, instead of asking:

“Give me social media ideas.”

A marketer could provide the target customer, product category, platform, campaign objective, brand personality, and content restrictions.

The result is more likely to fit the actual marketing situation.

Prompt Engineering for the AI Era + Toolkit E-books

AI Prompts for SEO Content

Search engine optimization requires more than inserting keywords into an article.

A useful AI prompt for SEO content can include:

· Primary keyword

· Secondary keywords

· Search intent

· Target audience

· Geographic market

· Article purpose

· Desired content structure

· Internal linking opportunities

· Frequently asked questions

· Brand tone

· Call to action

For example, an SEO content prompt might instruct the AI to create an article for small business owners searching for practical ways to improve local search visibility.

The prompt can then request an introduction, logical H2 and H3 sections, examples, FAQs, actionable recommendations, and a concise conclusion.

AI should still be treated as an assistant rather than an automatic publishing system. Human review remains important for accuracy, originality, brand consistency, and factual claims.

Prompt Engineering for Entrepreneurs

Entrepreneurs often have limited time and resources.

One person may need to handle marketing, customer support, product development, sales, research, and administration.

AI can help reduce some of this workload.

With carefully designed prompts, an entrepreneur can use an AI assistant to help create:

· Business plans

· Customer personas

· Value propositions

· Product descriptions

· Sales scripts

· Email sequences

· FAQ pages

· Meeting agendas

· Market research frameworks

· Customer interview questions

· Content strategies

· Standard operating procedures

· Business process documentation

For example, an entrepreneur launching a digital product could ask AI to evaluate the product positioning from the perspective of a potential customer.

A strong prompt might request three separate perspectives:

1. What would make the offer attractive?

2. What objections might a buyer have?

3. What information is missing from the current sales message?

This type of structured questioning can be more useful than simply asking AI to “improve my sales page.”

Prompt Engineering for Consultants

Consultants regularly transform complex information into practical recommendations.

That makes AI prompting particularly useful for research and analysis workflows.

A consultant might provide:

· Client background

· Business objectives

· Market information

· Existing challenges

· Constraints

· Available resources

· Relevant data

The AI can then help organize the information into categories, identify patterns, generate questions, or create a preliminary framework.

For example:

“Review the information below and identify the five most significant operational problems. For each problem, provide evidence from the supplied information, potential causes, business consequences, and questions that should be answered before recommending a solution.”

This prompt separates observation from interpretation and recommendation.

That is an important habit when using AI for professional work.

Prompt Engineering for Knowledge Workers

Knowledge workers spend much of their day dealing with information.

Managers, analysts, researchers, project coordinators, writers, HR professionals, educators, and administrators can all use AI to reduce repetitive cognitive tasks.

Common applications include:

Summarizing Long Information

Instead of simply requesting a summary, specify what matters.

For example:

“Summarize this report for a senior manager. Focus on major findings, risks, financial implications, unresolved issues, and recommended next steps. Keep the summary under 500 words.”

Turning Notes Into Action Items

AI can organize meeting notes into:

· Decisions

· Tasks

· Owners

· Deadlines

· Open questions

· Follow-up items

Comparing Options

A structured comparison prompt can request:

· Advantages

· Disadvantages

· Costs

· Risks

· Implementation requirements

· Key assumptions

This makes AI output easier to review and use.

The Power of Prompt Templates

One of the most practical concepts in prompt engineering is the reusable template.

Instead of writing a completely new prompt every time, create a framework with replaceable fields.

For example:

Role: You are a [professional role].
Context: [background information].
Objective: [desired outcome].
Audience: [target audience].
Task: [specific task].
Requirements: [constraints].
Format: [desired output structure].
Quality standard: [what a successful answer should achieve].

A template like this can become part of a professional’s daily workflow.

A marketer can adapt it for blog content, email campaigns, advertisements, and customer research.

A consultant can adapt it for research summaries, client presentations, and strategic analysis.

An entrepreneur can use it for product positioning, sales copy, customer communication, and business planning.

Prompt Chaining: Breaking Complex Tasks Into Steps

Large tasks can sometimes produce inconsistent results when everything is requested in one enormous prompt.

A better approach is to divide the workflow into stages.

For example, when creating an article:

Step 1: Define the target audience.

Step 2: Identify the reader’s main problems.

Step 3: Create a content outline.

Step 4: Develop each section.

Step 5: Review the content for missing information.

Step 6: Edit for clarity and consistency.

Step 7: Optimize the final version for search intent.

This process is often called prompt chaining.

The advantage is control.

Instead of accepting one large response, the user can review each stage and correct direction before continuing.

Few-Shot Prompting and Examples

Examples can be powerful when you need a specific style or structure.

Suppose a company wants AI to classify customer messages into categories.

Instead of only describing the categories, provide examples:

Customer message: “The package arrived two days late.”
Category: Delivery Issue

Customer message: “I was charged twice for the same order.”
Category: Billing Issue

Then provide the new messages and ask the AI to classify them.

This technique, often referred to as few-shot prompting, gives the model examples of the desired behavior.

It can be useful for:

· Content classification

· Customer support

· Tone matching

· Formatting

· Categorization

· Data labeling

· Repetitive business workflows

Prompt Engineering for the AI Era + Toolkit E-books

AI Prompting for Better Business Writing

Writing is one of the easiest areas in which professionals can benefit from structured prompts.

AI can help transform rough notes into:

· Professional emails

· Proposals

· Reports

· Presentations

· Executive summaries

· Customer responses

· LinkedIn posts

· Website copy

· Internal documentation

However, simply saying “make this professional” may remove the personality from the original message.

A better prompt can define the desired communication style:

“Rewrite this message for a busy executive. Keep the main points unchanged, remove unnecessary wording, use a confident but respectful tone, and make the requested action clear within the first two sentences.”

This gives the AI measurable editing goals.

AI Prompts for Productivity

AI is also useful as a personal productivity assistant.

A professional can use prompts to organize a busy workload.

For example:

“Here is my task list. Group the tasks by urgency and business impact. Identify tasks that can be delegated, combined, or postponed. Then create a realistic work plan for the next two business days.”

The output should not replace professional judgment, but it can provide a structured starting point.

Other productivity applications include:

· Daily planning

· Weekly reviews

· Meeting preparation

· Email prioritization

· Project planning

· Brainstorming

· Decision frameworks

· Learning plans

· Personal knowledge management

How to Reduce Weak AI Responses

Poor AI results often come from unclear expectations.

Common problems include:

Vague Instructions

“Write something about AI.”

There is no clear audience, purpose, or desired outcome.

Missing Context

AI cannot reliably infer important details that were never provided.

Too Many Objectives

Asking AI to research, analyze, write, edit, fact-check, optimize, and summarize everything at once can create inconsistent results.

No Output Format

If you do not specify the format, the AI chooses one.

No Quality Criteria

If you do not explain what “good” means, the AI has limited guidance for evaluating the result.

Improving these areas can significantly improve the usefulness of AI-generated content.

The Importance of Human Review

Effective prompt engineering does not mean allowing AI to operate without supervision.

AI systems can make mistakes. They may misunderstand context, generate inaccurate information, use outdated information, or produce statements that sound convincing but are not adequately supported.

Professional users should therefore review important outputs.

For business applications, review is particularly important when content involves:

· Financial decisions

· Legal matters

· Medical information

· Security

· Confidential business information

· Customer data

· Regulatory requirements

· Public claims

· Important strategic decisions

AI can accelerate work, but responsibility for the final result should remain with the human professional using the system.

AI Privacy and Confidential Information

Another important part of responsible AI use is information security.

Before entering company information into an AI system, professionals should understand their organization’s policies and the relevant platform’s data-handling practices.

Avoid casually entering:

· Passwords

· Private customer information

· Confidential contracts

· Sensitive employee information

· Proprietary business secrets

· Unreleased financial information

· Other restricted data

A good prompt can be technically excellent and still create problems if it contains information that should not have been shared.

Prompt engineering should therefore be considered alongside privacy, security, and responsible AI practices.

Building a Personal Prompt Library

One of the most valuable long-term habits is creating a personal prompt library.

Instead of starting from scratch every day, save prompts that consistently produce useful results.

Organize them into categories such as:

Marketing

· Blog writing

· SEO planning

· Social media

· Email campaigns

· Customer research

Business

· Business plans

· Product positioning

· Competitor analysis

· Process documentation

Productivity

· Meeting summaries

· Task planning

· Project organization

Communication

· Professional emails

· Proposals

· Reports

· Customer responses

Research

· Summaries

· Comparison frameworks

· Question generation

· Information organization

Over time, this library can become a practical personal AI productivity system.

What Makes Prompt Engineering for the AI Era + Toolkit Different?

Prompt Engineering for the AI Era + Toolkit E-books are designed around a straightforward problem: many professionals want to use AI more effectively but do not know where to start.

The goal is not to require programming knowledge.

The focus is practical AI use for people who need results in their everyday work.

The toolkit approach is particularly useful because professionals rarely need just one prompt.

They need repeatable systems.

A marketer may need prompts for research, content planning, SEO, social media, and email marketing.

A consultant may need prompts for analysis, presentations, client communication, and research.

An entrepreneur may need prompts for product development, marketing, sales, customer support, and operations.

A knowledge worker may need prompts for summarization, organization, writing, planning, and information analysis.

A collection of practical examples and reusable frameworks can reduce the amount of trial and error required to build these workflows independently.

Who Can Benefit From a Prompt Engineering Toolkit?

This type of resource can be useful for a broad range of non-technical professionals.

Marketing Professionals

Marketers can use prompt frameworks for content strategy, customer research, SEO, advertising, email marketing, and campaign planning.

Consultants

Consultants can apply structured prompts to research, analysis, reports, presentations, and client communication.

Entrepreneurs

Business owners can use AI to support marketing, planning, customer service, product development, and administrative tasks.

Freelancers

Freelancers can use AI prompts to accelerate proposals, content creation, client communication, research, and project organization.

Managers

Managers can use AI to prepare meeting agendas, organize notes, structure reports, and create communication drafts.

Writers and Content Creators

Creators can use prompting techniques to generate ideas, develop outlines, edit drafts, repurpose content, and adapt messaging for different audiences.

Students and Lifelong Learners

Prompting can also help learners create study plans, request explanations, practice questions, summarize materials, and explore unfamiliar subjects.

From Random AI Use to a Repeatable Workflow

There is a major difference between occasionally asking an AI chatbot a question and developing a repeatable AI workflow.

Random AI use might look like this:

“Help me write this.”

A repeatable workflow looks more like:

Input → AI processing → Human review → Revision → Final output

For example, a content marketer might build this process:

Research → Audience analysis → Outline → Draft → SEO review → Fact review → Final edit

Once the prompts for each stage are saved, the process becomes easier to repeat.

This is where prompt engineering can have practical business value.

The objective is not simply to generate more AI content.

The objective is to reduce wasted effort and make useful work easier to produce.

Learning Prompt Engineering Without a Technical Background

You do not need to understand machine learning algorithms to begin using prompt engineering.

Start with ordinary communication principles.

Ask yourself:

What do I want?

Who is the output for?

What information does the AI need?

What should the result look like?

What limitations should apply?

How will I judge whether the answer is useful?

These questions are more important for many everyday AI applications than technical terminology.

You can improve quickly by testing one prompt, reviewing the output, identifying what was missing, and revising the instructions.

This process turns prompting into a practical professional skill rather than a theoretical subject.

A Simple Prompt Engineering Workflow

A useful five-step process is:

Step 1: Define the Outcome

Start with the result you actually need.

Step 2: Provide Context

Give AI the information necessary to understand the situation.

Step 3: Add Constraints

Specify audience, tone, length, limitations, and required information.

Step 4: Define the Output

Tell the AI exactly how you want the response organized.

Step 5: Review and Refine

Examine the result and adjust the prompt based on what is missing.

This final step is important.

Prompt engineering is iterative.

The first prompt does not need to be perfect. The goal is to create a process in which each revision improves the usefulness of the result.

The Future of AI Skills at Work

AI is becoming part of everyday professional workflows.

The people who benefit most may not necessarily be those with the deepest technical knowledge. Many practical AI applications depend on understanding business objectives, customer needs, communication, decision-making, and workflow design.

That creates an opportunity for non-technical professionals.

Someone who already understands marketing can combine marketing expertise with AI prompting.

A consultant can combine industry knowledge with AI-assisted analysis.

An entrepreneur can combine business judgment with AI productivity tools.

A writer can combine editorial skills with AI-assisted drafting and revision.

The human expertise remains important. AI becomes an additional layer that can help process information and accelerate certain tasks.

Final Thoughts

Prompt engineering has moved beyond the world of programmers and AI researchers.

For modern professionals, it can be a practical method for communicating with AI systems more effectively.

Whether you use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or another AI assistant, the same fundamental principles are useful: define the objective, provide context, explain the task, set appropriate constraints, specify the desired format, and review the final result.

The real value of AI is not simply producing more text or generating more answers.

It is helping people spend less time on repetitive work and more time on activities that require judgment, creativity, experience, and human decision-making.

Prompt Engineering for the AI Era + Toolkit E-books provides a practical starting point for professionals who want to build that capability without learning programming or complicated technical concepts.

For marketers, consultants, entrepreneurs, freelancers, writers, managers, and other knowledge workers, learning how to communicate effectively with AI can become an important part of modern digital productivity.

The most useful prompt is rarely the longest prompt. It is the one that clearly communicates the goal, supplies the right context, and produces an output that can actually be used.

As AI tools continue to evolve, the ability to work with them effectively can become a valuable professional skill. A practical prompt toolkit gives non-technical users a structured way to develop that skill, create repeatable workflows, and make AI a more useful part of everyday work.

medium.resumo: I set out to build a proper shortcuts library, not a toy. I hand-wrote the React core, then used Claude Code to take it to six frameworks…
medium.conteudo_html:
I set out to build a proper shortcuts library, not a toy. I hand-wrote the React core, then used Claude Code to take it to six frameworks in record time. Then npm nearly filibustered both of us at the finish line.

Full disclosure, right up top: I wrote the original React hook myself, by hand, no assistance. Everything past that (turning it into a proper package, generalizing it to five more frameworks, writing the test suite, and hunting down the bugs below) was done with Claude Code. I’m not burying that in a footnote. It’s the actual subject of this post.

This didn’t start as a weekend hack that accidentally grew legs. I sat down wanting to build a real shortcuts library, the kind of thing that could declare keyboard, mouse, and wheel shortcuts as plain strings, things like "CTRL+SHIFT+F", "CMD+Z", "DOUBLE_LEFT_BUTTON", and wire them up to handlers without a single hand-rolled addEventListener anywhere in your app. I built the React core myself, from scratch, no assistance. That part was always going to be React-only in my head, at first, a solid foundation before anything else.

But “something big” was the goal from day one, not an afterthought, and a shortcuts library that only works in React isn’t big, it’s a hook with a README. So rather than spend weeks personally relearning the lifecycle quirks of five frameworks I don’t use day to day, I brought in Claude Code and pointed it at the goal directly: take this React implementation and turn it into a real, multi-framework package. Quickly. What came back, and how fast it came back, is the actual subject of this post, including the part where the framework support turned out to be the easy half and the real work was a build tool arguing with itself and npm’s auth system treating us both like we were smuggling a package past customs.

TL;DR

  • The goal from day one was a real, multi-framework shortcuts library, not a side hook.
  • I wrote the React core by hand. Claude Code did the rest of what’s below, fast.
  • It pulled the event-handling logic into one framework-agnostic ShortcutsManager class.
  • Then wrote a thin adapter for each framework as its own subpath export: /react, /vue, /svelte, /solid, /preact, /angular.
  • Its own test suite caught two genuinely funny bugs in its own adapters, and fixed both.
  • Publishing got blocked by 2FA, then by a stale global npm token, then by a token scoped to the wrong account. In that order. On the same package.
  • It’s live: npm install browser-shortcuts.

01 One core, six costumes

The instinct when you want to “support more frameworks” is to go rewrite the library six times. Claude Code’s instinct, thankfully, was to resist that: six slightly-different implementations means six slightly-different bugs, forever. Instead it pulled the entire event-listening brain out of my original hook, the part that listens on window, normalizes a KeyboardEvent into a string like "CTRL+SHIFT+F", and dispatches it to listeners, into a plain class with no framework opinions at all.

class ShortcutsManager {
  on(shortcut, callback) { /* register */ }
  off(shortcut, callback) { /* unregister */ }
  attach(target = window) { /* returns a disposer */ }
}

Every framework adapter is now just this class wearing a costume appropriate to its house party: React kept my original Context Provider and useShortcut hook, rebuilt on top of the shared core. Vue got a plugin and a composable. Svelte got setupShortcuts() plus a hook that reads Svelte's context. Solid got a Provider built on its own context primitive. Angular got an injectable singleton service with DestroyRef-powered cleanup. Preact got, and I want you to sit with how funny this is, the exact same code as React, because Preact's hooks API is basically a very polite tribute act.

react preact vue svelte solid angular

One brain, six faces, and a tsup config with seven separate build entries so nobody importing browser-shortcuts/svelte accidentally drags React into their bundle.

02 The bugs were the fun part

Claude Code wrote a vitest suite that exercises the core and all six adapters: mount, fire the shortcut, unmount, confirm it stopped firing. Thirty-two tests. Along the way that suite turned up two bugs in its own freshly-written code, which it then diagnosed and fixed without me touching a line. Watching an AI catch and root-cause its own bugs is a strange kind of satisfying, like watching someone proofread their own essay out loud and actually catch the typos.

⚠ Bug 01

Solid cleaned up a cleanup function that didn’t exist

This one took the longest to run down, and it’s the kind of bug that makes you question your grip on reality. The Solid provider called onCleanup() to remove its event listeners on unmount. It compiled fine. It ran fine. It just... never actually cleaned up. No error, no warning most of the time, just a listener that outlived the component that created it.

The actual cause: in the test environment, solid-js and solid-js/web were being loaded as two separate module instances, each with its own private copy of Solid's internal "current owner" tracking variable. The component's onCleanup call registered against one copy of that variable; the root's dispose() function tore down the other. Two universes, politely ignoring each other.

Fix: since these components render no real DOM, Claude Code stopped going through solid-js/web's render() in tests entirely and drove everything through solid-js's own createRoot instead: one module, one owner, one universe.

⚠ Bug 02

Angular’s tests demanded a hazing ritual

To test one @Injectable class, it needed: zone.js (Angular's change-detection engine, which apparently just refuses to exist without it), @angular/compiler (for JIT test compilation), @angular/platform-browser-dynamic, a TestBed.initTestEnvironment() call, and a fight with Vite 8's new decorator transform before any of that would even parse. Angular decorators plus a brand-new test bundler is apparently not a combination anyone has smoothed over yet.

Fix: all of the above, added one at a time, in the order the error messages demanded them. Angular testing is basically Dark Souls with dependency injection, and I mean that as a compliment.

If your test suite doesn’t surprise you at least once, you didn’t test hard enough, and it doesn’t matter who, or what, wrote the tests.

03 Publishing: the real boss fight

Writing six framework adapters was, weirdly, the calm part of this project. The final boss was npm publish.

Round one: a flat 403, "Two-factor authentication or granular access token with bypass 2FA enabled is required to publish packages." Fine, I made a token with bypass-2FA explicitly enabled. Still failed.

Round two: turns out the token I’d carefully configured in my project’s .npmrc was being silently ignored, because the package lives inside an npm workspace and npm refuses to read a workspace member's own .npmrc for auth. The token actually being used was a stale one sitting in my global ~/.npmrc, created before I'd ever heard the words "bypass 2FA."

The actual lesson: most auth failures aren’t “is this credential valid,” they’re “which credential is even being sent.” Check that first. It’ll save you a lot of staring at error messages that are technically true but pointing at the wrong culprit.

Round three: fixed the global token, got a brand new error: a 404 on a package name that definitely exists. Turned out the new token had been scoped to the wrong account context during setup. Once that was sorted, the actual publish took about four seconds. The npm CLI does not care how much of an emotional journey you just had.

04 If you’re staring at your own single-framework library

Here’s the encouraging part, because this whole post could read like a cautionary tale and it isn’t one: generalizing a library across frameworks is genuinely more approachable than it looks from the outside, and it’s a legitimately good use of an AI pair. The pattern (one core, thin adapters) is well-established, the failure modes are well-documented across enough GitHub issues to be learnable, and the tests catch you the moment you drift. You don’t need a grand unifying abstraction. You need one honest class that does the actual work, and the discipline to keep every framework’s adapter dumb, just lifecycle glue, nothing clever. The moment an adapter starts containing real logic, you’ve built six libraries again, not one.

And write the tests, whoever’s writing the code. Not because tests are virtuous, but because they’re the fastest way to find out where the mental model of “how this framework works” is quietly wrong. Both bugs above were a gap between what was assumed and what was actually true, and they only surfaced because a test insisted on checking.

I’ll say the quiet part plainly, since it’s the actual point of this post: I wrote the React hook, Claude Code wrote the rest of what’s above, and I’m comfortable putting my name on both halves. It’s live now, MIT-licensed, zero runtime dependencies of its own:

npm install browser-shortcuts
  • browser-shortcuts/react and /preact: a Provider and a useShortcut hook
  • browser-shortcuts/vue: a plugin and a composable
  • browser-shortcuts/svelte: setupShortcuts() plus a hook
  • browser-shortcuts/solid: a context Provider
  • browser-shortcuts/angular: an injectable service

If you use one of these frameworks and shortcuts in your app currently involve a stray addEventListener in a useEffect somewhere, I'd love for you to try it and tell me what breaks. That's genuinely the fastest way to find bug number three.

Side note

This isn’t the first thing I’ve shipped to npm, and it won’t be the last. If you’re curious what else is out there:

  • antoniookoro.com, my portfolio, with writing, projects, and how to reach me
  • vue3-form, form validation for Vue 3 and the composition API
  • bootstrap-vue-datatable, a datatable plugin for Vue and Bootstrap
  • storagedotjs, a small, lightweight API over Local Storage

Written by Antonio Okoro, built with Claude Code.
Thoughts, bug reports, and “well actually”s about Solid’s owner tracking are all welcome.

medium.titulo: Building Accessible Vue Components: A Developer-First Approach
medium.resumo: Practical patterns for making accessibility part of component development before issues reach QA or production.
medium.conteudo_html:
Practical patterns for making accessibility part of component development before issues reach QA or production.

In my previous article, Shifting Accessibility Left: Bringing Accessibility Into the Developer Workflow, I discussed a simple idea: accessibility feedback becomes much more useful when it reaches developers while software is being built.

But what does that actually look like in code?

For front-end developers, one of the most effective places to start is the component layer.

Modern applications are built from reusable pieces. Buttons, inputs, modals, dropdowns, cards, navigation elements, and entire interaction patterns are implemented once and reused throughout an application.

That creates an interesting consequence.

When an accessibility problem exists inside a reusable component, the problem scales. When accessibility is built into that component correctly, the solution scales too.

That is why accessible component development should be treated as an engineering concern rather than something we only look at during QA.

Let’s look at what that means in practice using Vue.

A component can work perfectly and still be inaccessible

Consider something as simple as a clickable element:

<template>
  <div
    class="button"
    @click="addToCart"
  >
    Add to Cart
  </div>
</template>

From a visual perspective, this can easily look like a button.

We can style it. We can attach a click handler. We can make it behave correctly with a mouse.

From a basic functional testing perspective, someone might conclude:

It works.

But that conclusion depends heavily on how the person interacts with the application.

A <div> does not automatically have button semantics. It is not keyboard-operable like a native button, and assistive technologies do not receive the same information they would receive from an actual <button>.

The simplest improvement is also the most important one:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="button"
    @click="addToCart"
  >
    Add to Cart
  </button>
</template>

This small change gives us a surprising amount of behavior for free.

The browser already understands what a button is. Keyboard interaction works as expected. Assistive technologies can identify the element correctly, and focus behavior follows established browser conventions.

This illustrates one of the most useful accessibility principles in front-end development:

Use native HTML semantics whenever they already describe the interaction you are building.

ARIA is extremely valuable, but it should not be used to recreate behavior that HTML already provides.

Accessibility starts at the component API

The problem becomes more interesting when we turn that button into a reusable component.

Imagine a generic icon button:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="icon-button"
    @click="$emit('click')"
  >
    <Icon :name="icon" />
  </button>
</template>

Visually, the icon may communicate the action perfectly.

A trash icon means delete. A magnifying glass means search. An X means close.

But visual meaning is not necessarily an accessible name.

We can expose that requirement through the component API:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="icon-button"
    :aria-label="label"
    @click="$emit('click')"
  >
    <Icon
      :name="icon"
      aria-hidden="true"
    />
  </button>
</template>
<script>
export default {
  props: {
    icon: {
      type: String,
      required: true
    },
    label: {
      type: String,
      required: true
    }
  }
}
</script>

Now the developer consuming the component has to provide the information it needs:

<IconButton
  icon="trash"
  label="Delete item"
/>

This changes something important in the architecture.

Instead of hoping every developer remembers to add accessibility later, we design the component so that using it correctly naturally encourages accessible behavior.

Accessibility becomes part of the component’s API contract.

Reusable components multiply decisions

Suppose an application uses the same button component in 100 different places.

If that component has poor keyboard behavior, we potentially created the same accessibility problem 100 times.

If we try to fix each implementation individually, we now have 100 places to verify and maintain.

But if the behavior belongs inside a shared component, a single improvement can propagate throughout the application.

The same principle applies to form controls, navigation, dropdowns, accordions, dialogs, tabs, notifications, tooltips, and interactive cards.

This is one reason design systems and component libraries can play such an important role in accessibility.

They are not just tools for visual consistency.

They are also distribution mechanisms for engineering decisions.

Accessibility is one of those decisions.

Keyboard support should not be an afterthought

Mouse interaction is usually the easiest path to test during development.

Click something.

It works.

Move on.

But a useful habit is to occasionally put the mouse aside and navigate the interface using only the keyboard.

There are a few simple questions worth asking:

Can I reach the interactive element with Tab?

Can I tell where the focus currently is?

Can I activate the control using the expected keyboard interaction?

Can I leave the component without getting trapped?

Does focus move somewhere unexpected after an action?

These checks become especially important when we build custom interactive components.

Consider a clickable product card:

<template>
  <div @click="openProduct(product)">
    <h3>{{ product.name }}</h3>
    <p>{{ product.description }}</p>
  </div>
</template>

It can be tempting to add tabindex, keyboard listeners, roles, and additional ARIA attributes until the <div> behaves like an interactive control.

Sometimes a custom interaction genuinely requires additional behavior.

But before doing that, there is a better engineering question to ask:

Is there already a native HTML element that represents this interaction?

If clicking the card performs navigation, perhaps the component should contain an <a>.

If it performs an action, perhaps it should use a <button>.

Choosing the correct semantic foundation can eliminate entire categories of accessibility bugs before they exist.

ARIA should add meaning, not compensate for architecture

ARIA is sometimes treated as the accessibility layer of an application.

That can lead to implementations like this:

<div
  role="button"
  tabindex="0"
  aria-label="Add to Cart"
>
  Add to Cart
</div>

The markup now communicates more information to assistive technology, but we have also taken responsibility for reproducing behavior that a native button already provides.

We may need to handle keyboard activation ourselves.

We need to maintain focus behavior.

We need to make sure different states are communicated correctly.

We also need to test those behaviors across browsers and assistive technologies.

Compare that with:

<button type="button">
  Add to Cart
</button>

The second implementation is not simply shorter.

It transfers responsibility for established interaction behavior back to the browser.

In most cases, that’s exactly what we want.

Start with semantic HTML. Use ARIA when additional semantics or state are actually necessary.

Accessible states matter too

Accessibility is not limited to the initial state of a component.

Modern interfaces constantly change.

Buttons become disabled. Forms display errors. Content loads asynchronously. Menus expand and collapse. Dialogs appear. Notifications are generated.

A component therefore needs to communicate not only what it is, but sometimes what is happening to it.

Consider a loading button:

<template>
  <button
    type="submit"
    :disabled="loading"
  >
    {{ loading ? 'Processing...' : 'Place Order' }}
  </button>
</template>

Changing the visible text is already useful.

Depending on the interaction, additional techniques may be appropriate for communicating asynchronous changes to assistive technologies.

But the larger engineering principle is more important:

Accessibility needs to follow component state.

If the UI changes visually but that change is not represented semantically, different users may effectively be interacting with different versions of the application.

Focus is part of application state

Dialogs are a good example.

Opening a modal is visually obvious.

For keyboard and screen reader users, however, focus management becomes part of the interaction.

When a dialog opens, we need to think about a few things.

Where should focus go?

Can the user navigate outside the dialog?

What happens when the dialog closes?

Should focus return to the element that opened it?

These aren’t just visual design details. They are part of the component’s behavior.

Once again, implementing this correctly inside a shared dialog component is much safer than asking every feature or developer to solve the same problem independently.

A well-designed component can encapsulate styles, markup, functionality, and accessible interaction behavior.

Accessibility belongs in the definition of a component

We often define component quality using characteristics such as reusable, responsive, performant, maintainable, and testable.

I believe accessible belongs on that list too.

A component that works only for a subset of interaction methods is not fully implemented.

This doesn’t mean every front-end developer needs to become an accessibility specialist.

It means accessibility should influence the same engineering decisions we already make every day.

Which HTML element should I use?

What should this component expose through props?

What states need to be represented?

How should keyboard interaction work?

Where should focus move?

Can this behavior be solved once inside the shared component instead of repeatedly across the application?

These are engineering questions.

And treating them that way changes when accessibility enters the development process.

Automated tools help, but they don’t understand everything

Linting, browser audits, automated accessibility testing, and CI checks can catch many common problems.

They can identify missing accessible names, invalid ARIA attributes, certain contrast issues, and some semantic problems.

These tools are valuable because they provide fast feedback.

But accessibility cannot be reduced to a score.

An automated tool cannot fully determine whether an interaction makes sense. It cannot always understand whether focus moves somewhere logical. It cannot guarantee that a complex workflow is understandable with a screen reader.

And most importantly, passing an automated accessibility test does not automatically mean the experience is usable.

Automation should support human judgment, not replace it.

What if this feedback appeared while we were coding?

This brings me back to the idea from my previous article.

Imagine writing a Vue component and receiving feedback directly inside the development environment:

AccessibleButton.vue

✓ Native button semantics
✓ Keyboard accessible
✓ Accessible name available
⚠ Focus state may not be visible
✓ No conflicting ARIA attributes

Instead of discovering these issues days or weeks later during QA, developers could address many of them while the component is still fresh in their minds.

Even more interestingly, tooling could understand component patterns rather than looking only at the final HTML.

It could analyze templates.

Props.

Interactive handlers.

ARIA usage.

Potential keyboard interactions.

Reusable component APIs.

That would move accessibility feedback closer to the moment when engineering decisions are actually being made.

And I think developer tooling still has a lot of room to explore here.

Build accessibility once, distribute it everywhere

Component-driven development gives us leverage.

That leverage works in both directions.

A poorly designed component can distribute accessibility problems across an entire product.

A thoughtfully designed component can distribute good accessibility practices just as efficiently.

Shifting accessibility left doesn’t necessarily mean adding another complicated stage to the development process.

Sometimes it starts with something much simpler.

Choosing a <button> instead of a <div>.

Making accessible names part of a component API.

Testing keyboard behavior before opening a pull request.

Managing focus inside shared interaction patterns.

Building accessibility into the components that other developers will reuse.

The earlier these decisions happen, the less accessibility feels like remediation.

It simply becomes part of building the component correctly.

That leaves me with another question I want to explore:

What if our development tools could help us make these decisions before the component ever leaves the editor?

That’s where I’d like to go next.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: A Maratona de Buenos Aires está cheia de brasileiros e agora tem a Blue Line da Adidas. Saiba os preços dos produtos oficiais e aprenda a pedir um corta-vento em espanhol. Veja a polêmica camiseta de Chicago e a confirmação de Bekele em Berlim.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sábado | 19 de setembro de 2026

Amanhã é dia da Maratona de Buenos Aires, prova que é carinhosamente chamada de “a melhor maratona do Brasil” por estar sempre lotada de brasileiros. A prova deste ano está mais internacional do que nunca, com 17,2% dos 16.384 inscritos sendo estrangeiros. E, como de costume, os brasileiros dominam essa fatia: somos 48% do total de corredores de fora da Argentina. A disputa para ser a maior maratona da América do Sul segue acirrada com a do Rio de Janeiro, que teve 14 mil concluintes este ano. A grande novidade em Buenos Aires é a estreia de uma “Blue Line” no asfalto, com as três listras da Adidas, patrocinadora da prova, assim como já acontece na Maratona de Berlim.

Quanto custa correr na Argentina? (E como pedir seu corta-vento)

Se você está na capital argentina para a maratona, pode estar se perguntando sobre os preços dos produtos oficiais na expo. Graças a um vídeo da corredora Thaís Tranto, temos os valores: uma camiseta oficial está custando 79.999 pesos (cerca de R$ 260), enquanto a jaqueta corta-vento sai por 129.999 pesos (aproximadamente R$ 430). E para não passar aperto na hora de comprar, anote aí: em espanhol, camiseta de corrida pode ser chamada de “remera” (ou “musculosa” se for regata) e o corta-vento é conhecido como “campera”.

Camiseta de finisher da Maratona de Chicago vira piada

A camiseta de finisher da Maratona de Chicago deste ano não agradou nem um pouco. A peça, em um tom de verde-limão bem chamativo e com a palavra “FINISHER” em uma fonte considerada simples, foi alvo de muitas críticas e memes nas redes sociais. Corredores reclamaram do design, comparando as letras a “desenhos de segunda série”. A repercussão negativa foi forte, com muitos lamentando a escolha da Nike para uma das maiores maratonas do mundo.

Bekele em Berlim e a briga pelo sub-2h em Valência

O lendário Kenenisa Bekele, aos 44 anos, foi confirmado na Maratona de Berlim. Ele, que tem um recorde pessoal de 2:01:41, retorna à prova onde já venceu duas vezes. Enquanto isso, a Maratona de Valência também promete fortes emoções. Yomif Kejelcha, o segundo homem a correr uma maratona abaixo de duas horas este ano em Londres, estará na prova. Além dele, John Korir, atleta da ASICS que venceu as maratonas de Chicago e Boston, também confirmou presença e declarou que seu objetivo é quebrar a barreira das duas horas, inspirado pelo feito em Londres. Com um bônus de 1 milhão de euros para quem bater o recorde mundial, a disputa em Valência será imperdível.

O rock pernambucano mais popular do streaming

No quiz de hoje, a pergunta foi sobre a música de rock pernambucano mais tocada nas plataformas de streaming. A resposta é “Maracatu Atômico”, do icônico Chico Science & Nação Zumbi, com impressionantes 26 milhões de plays. Como diz a letra, “uma cerveja antes do almoço é muito bom pra ficar pensando melhor”.
